cim: Astra for Law leads in legal intelligence
cim_eredeti: Astra for Law leads in legal intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Our latest model configuration earned leading marks on multiple benchmarks. Every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can now request access.

Today, we're releasing an updated Astra for Law that is state-of-the-art on Harvey LAB-AA and a top performer on LAB: USCL (co-developed by Harvey⁠(opens in a new window) and Grubel⁠(opens in a new window)) and Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench. We are also enabling all ChatGPT Enterprise customers to request access through the Trusted Access Program, including through the API.

Astra for Law is a model configuration of GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠, our latest, most powerful frontier model. It pairs GPT‑6.2 Astra with an expanded legal search index and instructions for researching a question, weighing the authorities, and writing the answer. Today’s configuration earned full credit on the LAB-AA tests nearly 40% more often than did the runner-up, GPT‑6.2 Astra.

Since we introduced Astra for Law in September⁠ to a small group of firms, including Cooley⁠, Ropes & Gray⁠ and Sullivan & Cromwell⁠, our research team has made rapid innovations to improve its legal reasoning and expand its legal search index by over a third. On Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window), the share of research answers that passed every check rose from about 46% to 53.8% in less than two months.

As the world grows more complex, lawyers occupy an increasingly important role. They shape nearly every system we rely on: they negotiate the agreements that move commerce, defend people’s rights in courts, and draft the laws we all live by. That’s why we’ve made law a research priority at OpenAI: to put the best intelligence in the hands of the best lawyers.

Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) tests whether a model can take a legal assignment from start to finish. LAB-AA⁠(opens in a new window) is Artificial Analysis’s version of that test. It puts the models through a ringer of 120 assignments developed by Harvey across 24 areas of law – everything from drafting deposition outlines to reviewing commercial leases to strategizing ownership changes in acquisitions. To earn full credit, an answer must meet every requirement of an assignment without hallucinating, i.e. making a material claim that is not supported by the source documents.

Astra for Law ranked first, earning full credit on 20.8% of assignments, ahead of GPT‑6.2 Astra at 15.0% and Muse Wonder Full at 13.1%.

Astra for Law ranked first at 20.8%, earning full credit about 59% more often than Muse Wonder Full, the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model.

Astra for Law also earned that top score with 54% less output per assignment than the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model in the evaluation, averaging about 64,000 output tokens per assignment, compared with 139,000 for Muse Wonder Full. For legal teams paying by usage, this can mean the difference between staying within budget and blowing through it.

Each dot is a model configuration. Higher means more assignments earned full credit; farther left means fewer output tokens, which include the text a model generates as it reasons and writes. Astra for Law averaged about 64,000 output tokens per assignment and earned full credit on 20.8%, compared with 139,000 and 13.1% for Muse Wonder Full. No configuration shown matched Astra for Law’s score using fewer output tokens.

Hallucinations are unacceptable in legal work. A single invented citation can cost a lawyer a client’s trust, credibility in court, and a reputation built over years. That’s why reducing hallucinations has been a priority for Astra for Law. In Artificial Analysis’s latest LAB-AA comparison, Astra for Law tied (with GPT‑6) for the lowest rate of material hallucinations: 0.03 per assignment, compared with 0.59 for Claude Opus 5.5 (the next lowest non-OpenAI model). Notably, Astra for Law's performance on this eval included zero material hallucinations for tasks that met the all-pass criteria.

Astra for Law averaged 0.03 material and 0.06 minor hallucinations per assignment. Claude Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material and 0.51 minor hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many material hallucinations and 8.5 times as many minor ones.

Across the same 120 assignments, Artificial Analysis counted hallucinated claims that could mislead a reader on a substantive point. Astra for Law averaged 0.03 such errors per assignment, tied for the lowest rate in the comparison and roughly half the rate for regular GPT‑6.2 Astra (0.06).

Every OpenAI configuration tested had fewer hallucinations than Claude Opus 5.5, the best non-OpenAI result on this measure. Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many as Astra for Law.

Brief writing is one of the most complex long-horizon processes in law, requiring clear reasoning, research, and writing to come together to produce an excellent argument.

Harvey and Grubel⁠(opens in a new window) co-developed LAB: USCL⁠(opens in a new window) to test whether a model can research and write a brief in a real U.S. federal case. Each model steps in just before a brief was filed and writes for the same party on the same issue. In one version, the model has to find the relevant cases itself. In the other, it gets the record and the precedents the original lawyer cited. AI graders compare the briefs head to head using criteria lawyers reviewed and calibrated. Astra for Law earned one of the top scores in both versions.

Farther right means the briefs earned higher ratings. When the models researched the law themselves, Astra for Law scored 1,844 to Opus 5.5’s 1,817. Given the precedents, they were effectively even at 1,883 and 1,882.

The first result (“Research and draft,” on the left) matters because better legal research is one of the core improvements in this release. We focused on improving this result because a litigator rarely starts with a list of the right cases. Here, each model had to work out which decisions mattered and use them to write an argument the court could follow. On that assignment, Harvey’s graders preferred the briefs from today’s Astra for Law to those from other leading frontier models, such as Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon. We can see more noticeable improvements in legal research in the Vals AI evaluation, discussed next.

We've made law a research priority at OpenAI, dedicating a team of researchers to accelerate innovation for frontier legal intelligence. One early measure of their progress comes from Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window), where practicing lawyers set questions about U.S. federal and state law. An answer has to cover every required point and pass the source checks. In September, Astra for Law earned full credit on about 46% of questions. In Vals AI’s November 16 evaluation, it earned full credit on 112 of 208 questions (53.8%), a gain of about eight percentage points in under two months. Across all questions, it earned 90.9% of the available points, including partial credit.

In less than two months, the share of legal research questions on which Astra for Law earned full credit rose from about 46% to 53.8%, a gain of about eight percentage points.

Astra for Law (green) sits in the small cluster of top performers on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench.

Building Astra for Law as a model configuration lets us stay on the bleeding edge of the frontier, in this case GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠. On top of this foundation, we iteratively refine Astra for Law’s specific settings and instructions in response to practitioner feedback, teaching it how to reason and write like a seasoned lawyer. We also continuously hone its tools, such as the legal search index. Since September, we’ve grown the index by 34%, adding over 80 million new URLs, including across international jurisdictions such as the UK, Australia and Canada. Today, the updated index spans over 310 million URLs and covers more than 99.9% of published U.S. precedential case law⁠(opens in a new window).
